hints: Notice the question says using only the gradient of a velocity-time graph, so ask what physical quantity that gradient represents.
Recall that for uniform acceleration the straight-line gradient is $a = (v-u)/t$ where $u$ is the intercept at $t=0$ and $v$ is the velocity at time $t$.
Check which listed equation contains only $v$, $u$, $a$ and $t$ and can be made by rearranging that gradient expression, without needing area $s$.
walkthrough: Identify the graph feature: on a velocity-time graph the gradient is the rate of change of velocity, which is acceleration $a$.
For uniform acceleration the graph is a straight line from $(0,u)$ to $(t,v)$, so gradient $= $ change in $y$ over change in $x = (v-u)/t$.
Set the gradient equal to acceleration: $a = (v-u)/t$.
Multiply by $t$ to give $at = v - u$, then add $u$ to both sides to give $v = u + at$.
The other equations all contain displacement $s$, which comes from the area under the velocity-time graph, so they cannot be obtained from gradient alone.
This rearranged gradient result matches $v = u + at$. This is option C

A.explanation: This uses displacement $s$ from the area under the velocity-time graph, not from the gradient alone.

B.explanation: This uses both the area under the graph and substitution for $v$, so it needs more than just the gradient.

C.explanation: Gradient of a velocity-time graph is acceleration $a = (v-u)/t$, which rearranges directly to $v = u + at$.

D.explanation: This is found by eliminating $t$ between the gradient equation and the area equation, so it needs area as well.
